entry.sum: $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B) = H_n(P_\bullet\otimes_RB)$, the left derived functors of the tensor product, measure how far $-\otimes_RB$ is from exact; they can be computed by resolving either variable, from flat resolutions, and locally. Over $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/n,B)$ is the $n$-torsion of $B$; in general a module is flat exactly when $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ against it vanishes, and Tor is the correction term in the Künneth formula.
entry.why: Vanishing of Tor is the standard test for flatness in commutative algebra, Tor computes Betti numbers and intersection multiplicities, and it is the correction term in the Künneth and universal coefficient theorems of topology.

links.note: Serre's intersection multiplicity is an alternating sum of lengths of $\mathrm{Tor}_i(A/I,A/J)$.

blocks.body:
Tensoring the injection $2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ gives the zero map $\mathbb{Z}/2\to\mathbb{Z}/2$: the tensor product is right exact but not exact. The groups $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B)$, the left derived functors of $\otimes$ ([[derived-functors]]), measure this failure; $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ is the kernel that is lost when an injection is tensored. Čech introduced Tor in 1935. Over $\mathbb{Z}$ only $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ is interesting and it measures torsion, which is where the name comes from; over other rings every degree can be non-zero.

This page defines Tor, computes it on cyclic modules and through the Koszul complex, proves that Tor detects flatness, collects the tools used in practice (colimits, flat resolutions, localisation), shows Serre's reading of Tor as a derived intersection, and proves the Künneth formula for a tensor product of complexes, in which Tor is the correction term. Commutative algebra papers such as Holanda-Miranda-Neto's state their hypotheses as vanishing of Tor between finitely generated modules over a local ring, Shekhar-Gupta ask when vanishing of all high Tor groups forces finite projective dimension, and Tang's paper has to check how Tor and flatness behave in a setting where projective modules need not be flat.

blocks.title: Tor: definition and first computations
blocks.body: Tor is the left derived functor of the tensor product. Over $\mathbb{Z}$ it only has one interesting degree, $\mathrm{Tor}_1 = \mathrm{Tor}$, which is the kernel lost when an injection is tensored; over general rings all degrees can be non-zero, as the $\mathbb{Z}/4$ computation in the dimension-shifting example of [[derived-functors]] showed. This section defines Tor, computes it on cyclic modules, and proves that it detects flatness; the next collects the tools used in practice.

blocks.title: Tor
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a right $R$-module and $B$ a left $R$-module (for commutative $R$ the distinction disappears). Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to A$ and set
$$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B) &= H_n(P_\bullet\otimes_RB)\\ &= L_n(-\otimes_RB)(A).\end{aligned}$$
So $\mathrm{Tor}_0^R(A,B) = A\otimes_RB$, $\mathrm{Tor}_n = 0$ for $n<0$, and $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(P,B) = 0$ for $n>0$ when $P$ is projective. By the balancing theorem of [[derived-functors]], the same groups are obtained by resolving $B$ instead: $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B)\cong H_n(A\otimes_RQ_\bullet)$ for a projective resolution $Q_\bullet\to B$. When $R$ is commutative, $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B)$ is an $R$-module, $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(B,A)$, and multiplication by $r$ on $\mathrm{Tor}$ agrees with multiplication by $r$ on either argument, so $\mathrm{Tor}$ is killed by $\mathrm{Ann}(A)+\mathrm{Ann}(B)$.

blocks.title: Tor against a non-zero-divisor
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be commutative, $x\in R$ a non-zero-divisor and $M$ an $R$-module. Then
$$\begin{gathered}\mathrm{Tor}_0^R(R/xR,M) = M/xM,\\ \mathrm{Tor}_1^R(R/xR,M) = \{m\in M: xm = 0\},\\ \mathrm{Tor}_n^R(R/xR,M) = 0\ (n\ge2).\end{gathered}$$
In particular, over $\mathbb{Z}$: $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/m,B) = B[m]$, the $m$-torsion of $B$, and $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/m,\mathbb{Z}/n)\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)$. This is where the name comes from: $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ measures torsion.

Since $x$ is a non-zero-divisor, $0\to R\xrightarrow{x}R\to R/xR\to0$ is a free resolution. Tensoring the complex $R\xrightarrow{x}R$ with $M$ gives $M\xrightarrow{x}M$ in degrees $1, 0$. Its homology is $M/xM$ in degree $0$, the kernel of multiplication by $x$ in degree $1$, and $0$ above. For $M = \mathbb{Z}/n$ and $x = m$, the elements of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ killed by $m$ are the multiples of $n/d$ where $d = \gcd(m,n)$, a cyclic group of order $d$.

blocks.title: Tor of two cyclic modules
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be commutative and $I,J$ ideals. Then $\mathrm{Tor}_0^R(R/I,R/J) = R/(I+J)$ and
$$\mathrm{Tor}_1^R(R/I,R/J)\cong(I\cap J)/IJ.$$

$R/I\otimes R/J\cong R/(I+J)$ by right exactness. For $\mathrm{Tor}_1$, apply the long exact Tor sequence (in the first variable) to $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$, tensored with $R/J$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\mathrm{Tor}_1(R,R/J) = 0\to\mathrm{Tor}_1(R/I,R/J)\to{}\\ &\qquad I\otimes R/J\to R\otimes R/J\to\cdots.\end{aligned}$$
Here $I\otimes R/J\cong I/IJ$ (right exactness applied to $0\to J\to R\to R/J\to0$ tensored with $I$, whose image of $I\otimes J$ in $I$ is $IJ$), and $R\otimes R/J = R/J$. The map $I/IJ\to R/J$ is induced by inclusion, so its kernel is $(I\cap J)/IJ$.

blocks.title: Tor detects flatness

blocks.body:
(1) implies (2): if $M$ is flat, $-\otimes M$ is exact, so applying it to a projective resolution $P_\bullet\to N$ gives an exact sequence $\cdots\to P_1\otimes M\to P_0\otimes M\to N\otimes M\to0$, whose homology in positive degrees is $\mathrm{Tor}_n(N,M)$. (2) implies (3) implies (4) trivially; for the reformulation of (4), the long exact sequence of $0\to I\to R\to R/I\to0$ gives
$$\begin{aligned}0 = \mathrm{Tor}_1(R,M)&\to\mathrm{Tor}_1(R/I,M)\\ &\to I\otimes M\to M.\end{aligned}$$

(4) implies (1). Write $X^+ = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(X,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})$. Two facts are needed. First, a homomorphism $u\colon X\to Y$ of abelian groups is injective if and only if $u^+\colon Y^+\to X^+$ is surjective: if $u$ is injective, $u^+$ is onto because $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is injective; if $u(x) = 0$ with $x\ne0$, pick a non-zero map $\mathbb{Z}x\to\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ (possible for a cyclic group), extend it to $X$ by injectivity, and observe that it is not of the form $\psi\circ u$. Second, Hom-tensor adjunction gives $(X\otimes_RM)^+\cong\mathrm{Hom}_R(X,M^+)$ naturally in the $R$-module $X$.

Now assume (4). For an ideal $I$, injectivity of $I\otimes M\to R\otimes M$ means, by the first fact, that $(R\otimes M)^+\to(I\otimes M)^+$ is onto, i.e. $\mathrm{Hom}_R(R,M^+)\to\mathrm{Hom}_R(I,M^+)$ is onto. By Baer's criterion ([[homological-algebra]]) $M^+$ is an injective $R$-module. Then for any injection $X\to Y$, the map $\mathrm{Hom}_R(Y,M^+)\to\mathrm{Hom}_R(X,M^+)$, which is $(Y\otimes M)^+\to(X\otimes M)^+$, is onto, so $X\otimes M\to Y\otimes M$ is injective by the first fact. So $M$ is flat.

Over a PID every ideal is $(r)$, and $(r)\otimes M\to M$ is identified with multiplication by $r$ on $M$ (for $r\ne0$, since $(r)\cong R$). It is injective for all $r\neq 0$ exactly when $M$ is torsion-free.

blocks.title: Computing Tor in practice
blocks.body:
Besides resolutions and long exact sequences, four properties do most of the work.

1. Additivity and colimits. Tor commutes with direct sums in each variable and, more generally, with filtered colimits (Wikipedia, Tor functor), because tensor products and homology do. For finitely generated abelian groups this reduces everything to cyclic groups: $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}/a_i,\ B) = \bigoplus B[a_i]$.
2. Flat resolutions. By the acyclic resolution argument of [[derived-functors]], $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B) = H_n(F_\bullet\otimes B)$ for any flat resolution $F_\bullet\to A$, and similarly in the other variable (Weibel's Flat Resolution Lemma 3.2.8).
3. Localisation. For commutative $R$ and a multiplicative set $S$, $S^{-1}R$ is flat over $R$ and $S^{-1}\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n^{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}A,S^{-1}B)$ (Weibel Theorem 3.2.2, and the flat base change Corollary 3.2.10 with $T = S^{-1}R$): localise a projective resolution of $A$, which stays a projective resolution because localisation is exact. So vanishing of Tor can be tested locally.
4. Finite projective dimension. If $A$ has a projective resolution $P_\bullet$ of length $n$, that is, projective dimension at most $n$ in the sense of [[ext]], then $P_\bullet\otimes B$ vanishes above degree $n$, so $\mathrm{Tor}_i(A,B) = 0$ for all $i>n$ and all $B$. Resolving the second variable instead (balancing) gives the same conclusion when $B$ has a projective resolution of length $n$. Over a Noetherian local ring, papers on Tor-vanishing ask for the converse: Shekhar and Gupta say that $R$ has the Tor-vanishing property if, for finitely generated $M$ and $N$, $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,N) = 0$ for all large $i$ forces $\mathrm{pd}_RM<\infty$ or $\mathrm{pd}_RN<\infty$.

Weibel's Proposition 3.1.3 is a typical application of the colimit property: $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},B)$ is the torsion subgroup of $B$. Indeed $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is the union of its subgroups $\frac1n\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/n$, and the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}/n\to\mathbb{Z}/nm$ (sending $1$ to $m$) lifts to the resolutions $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{nm}\mathbb{Z}$ by the identity in degree $1$ and multiplication by $m$ in degree $0$. On $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ it therefore induces the inclusion $B[n]\subseteq B[nm]$, and the colimit is $\bigcup_nB[n]$, the torsion subgroup.

blocks.title: Tor over a polynomial ring: the Koszul complex
blocks.body:
Let $k$ be a field, $R = k[x,y]$ and $k = R/(x,y)$. Show that
$$0\to R\xrightarrow{\begin{pmatrix}-y\\ x\end{pmatrix}}R^2\xrightarrow{(x\ \ y)}R\to k\to0$$
is a free resolution, and compute $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(k,k)$ and $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(k,R/(x))$.
blocks.solution:
The composite of the two matrices is $-xy+yx = 0$. Exactness at $R$: the image of $(x\ y)$ is the ideal $(x,y)$, the kernel of $R\to k$. Exactness at $R^2$: if $xf+yg = 0$ then $x\mid g$ because $x,y$ are coprime in the UFD $R$; writing $g = xh$ gives $f = -yh$, so $(f,g) = h(-y,x)$. The left map is injective since $R$ is a domain.

Tensor with $k$: every entry of both matrices lies in $(x,y)$, so all differentials become zero, and
$$\mathrm{Tor}_0(k,k) = k,\quad\mathrm{Tor}_1(k,k) = k^2,\quad\mathrm{Tor}_2(k,k) = k,$$
with dimensions $\binom{2}{i}$: the exterior algebra on two generators, as Wikipedia notes for the polynomial ring in $n$ variables (where the Koszul complex has $\binom{n}{i}$ free summands in degree $i$).

Tensor with $R/(x)\cong k[y]$ instead: the complex becomes $k[y]\xrightarrow{(-y,\ 0)^T}k[y]^2\xrightarrow{(0\ \ y)}k[y]$. Homology: in degree $0$, $k[y]/(y) = k$; in degree $1$, the kernel of $(f,g)\mapsto yg$ is $\{(f,0)\}$, and the image of the first map is $\{(-yh,0)\}$, so $\mathrm{Tor}_1 = k[y]/(y) = k$; in degree $2$, the first map is injective, so $\mathrm{Tor}_2 = 0$. This agrees with the non-zero-divisor theorem applied with the roles swapped: $\mathrm{Tor}_i(R/(x),k)$ is $k/xk = k$, the $x$-torsion of $k$, which is $k$, and $0$.

blocks.title: Tor as a derived intersection
blocks.body: Serre's formula defines the intersection multiplicity of two subvarieties $V(I), V(J)$ at a point as $\sum_i(-1)^i\,\mathrm{length}\,\mathrm{Tor}_i^A(A/I,A/J)$, with $A$ the local ring at the point. Compute the terms for the parabola $y = x^2$ and its tangent line $y = 0$ in $R = k[x,y]$ (localising at the origin changes nothing here), and for the line $x = 0$ against itself.
blocks.solution:
Let $I = (y)$, $J = (y-x^2)$. Then $\mathrm{Tor}_0 = R/(y,\,y-x^2) = k[x]/(x^2)$, of length $2$. For the higher terms, $y-x^2$ is a non-zero-divisor on $R/(y)\cong k[x]$ (it acts as $-x^2$), so by the non-zero-divisor theorem $\mathrm{Tor}_1(R/J,R/I)$ is the $(y-x^2)$-torsion of $k[x]$, which is $0$, and the higher Tor vanish. The multiplicity is $2$, the expected answer for a tangency, and here the naive length of $A/I\otimes A/J$ is already right.

For $I = J = (x)$: $\mathrm{Tor}_0 = R/(x) = k[y]$ and, by the cyclic-module theorem, $\mathrm{Tor}_1 = (x)/(x^2)\cong R/(x)$, which is non-zero. The two copies of the line do not meet properly: these groups have infinite length, so Serre's formula does not apply, and the non-zero $\mathrm{Tor}_1$ records the excess intersection. When both subvarieties are locally cut out by regular sequences and meet properly, all higher Tor vanish and only $\mathrm{Tor}_0$ survives, as in the first computation.

blocks.caption: The parabola y = x^2 and its tangent line y = 0 meet at one point with multiplicity 2, the length of Tor_0 = k[x]/(x^2); all higher Tor vanish. A nearby line y = c (c > 0) meets the parabola in two distinct points.

blocks.title: What Tor measures
blocks.body: Four sources, four pictures of the same groups.

items.label: Torsion
items.body: $\mathrm{Tor}_1(R/x,M)$ is the $x$-torsion of $M$, $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/n,A) = A[n]$ and $\mathrm{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},B)$ is the whole torsion subgroup; and $\mathrm{Tor}_1(A,-) = 0$ exactly for torsion-free $A$ over $\mathbb{Z}$. This is the origin of the name.

items.label: Lost injectivity
items.body: Tensoring an injection can produce a non-injective map, and Tor records the kernel: for $0\to F_1\to F_0\to A\to0$ free, $\mathrm{Tor}(A,M) = \ker(F_1\otimes M\to F_0\otimes M)$. Quick's lecture shows that multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ becomes zero after $\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2$, and defines Tor over $\mathbb{Z}$ as exactly this kind of kernel.

items.label: Derived intersection
items.body: For ideals $I,J$, $A/I\otimes A/J = A/(I+J)$ is the ring of the naive intersection; the higher $\mathrm{Tor}_i(A/I,A/J)$ correct it, and Serre's alternating sum of their lengths is the intersection multiplicity.

items.label: Balanced bifunctor
items.body: Tor is the homology of the total complex of $P_\bullet\otimes Q_\bullet$, which treats both variables alike; nLab presents Tor as the homology of the derived tensor product, and the Michigan notes use the double complex to prove the symmetry $\mathrm{Tor}_n(M,N)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(N,M)$.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/12\oplus\mathbb{Z}/18,\ \mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z})$.
2. Show that $\mathrm{Tor}_1^{\mathbb{Z}}(A,B)$ is a torsion group for all $A,B$ (write $A$ as a filtered colimit of finitely generated subgroups).
3. Let $R = k[x,y]$ and $I = (x)$, $J = (y)$. Compute $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(R/I,R/J)$ for all $i$, and compare with $(I\cap J)/IJ$.
4. Over $R = k[x]/(x^2)$, compute $\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(k,k)$ for all $n$ and compare with the $\mathbb{Z}/4$ example on [[derived-functors]].
5. Show that $\mathrm{Tor}^{\mathbb{Z}}_1(\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: Künneth formula for complexes
blocks.body: Tor first appeared as a correction term in topology. The homology of a tensor product of two complexes is not the tensor product of their homologies, and the Künneth formula identifies the difference as a sum of Tor groups. With one of the complexes a single module in degree $0$, it is the first universal coefficient theorem for homology with coefficients, which is proved together with its cohomological partner on [[ext]].

blocks.title: Künneth formula for a tensor product of complexes
blocks.body:
Let $P$ be a chain complex of free abelian groups and $Q$ any chain complex of abelian groups. The tensor product complex has $(P\otimes Q)_n = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}P_p\otimes Q_q$ and $d(a\otimes b) = da\otimes b+(-1)^pa\otimes db$ for $a\in P_p$. For every $n$ there is a short exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}&0\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)\to H_n(P\otimes Q){}\\ &\qquad\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\mathrm{Tor}(H_p(P),H_q(Q))\to0,\end{aligned}$$
and it splits, though not naturally. (Weibel Theorem 3.6.3, stated there over any ring for $P$ with $P_n$ and $d(P_n)$ flat; the splitting is asserted for free complexes over $\mathbb{Z}$.) Taking $Q = M$ in degree $0$ recovers the first universal coefficient sequence (see [[ext]]).

Weibel's proof is that of the universal coefficient theorem ([[ext]]) with $Q$ in place of $M$. Put $Z_p = \ker d_p$ and $B_p = \operatorname{im}d_{p+1}\subseteq Z_p$, both free as subgroups of free groups. Give $Z$ and $B$ the zero differential, and let $B^-$ denote $B$ moved up one degree, $B^-_p = B_{p-1}$. Then $d$ defines a chain map $P\to B^-$, and $0\to Z\to P\to B^-\to0$ is a short exact sequence of complexes, split in each degree because $B_{p-1}$ is free. Tensoring with $Q$ therefore keeps it exact:
$$0\to Z\otimes Q\to P\otimes Q\to B^-\otimes Q\to0.$$
As $Z$ has zero differential, $Z\otimes Q$ is the direct sum over $p$ of the complexes $Z_p\otimes Q$ (shifted by $p$, with differential $\pm1\otimes d$), and $Z_p\otimes-$ is exact because $Z_p$ is free, so it commutes with homology: $H_n(Z\otimes Q) = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}Z_p\otimes H_q(Q)$. In the same way $H_{n+1}(B^-\otimes Q) = \bigoplus_{p+q=n}B_p\otimes H_q(Q)$.

The connecting map $H_{n+1}(B^-\otimes Q)\to H_n(Z\otimes Q)$ is $\iota\otimes1$ on each summand, for the inclusion $\iota\colon B_p\to Z_p$: given $b\otimes z$ with $b\in B_p$ and $z$ a cycle of $Q_q$, lift it to $c\otimes z$ with $dc = b$, and apply $d$ to get $b\otimes z\pm c\otimes dz = b\otimes z$. By the long exact sequence, $H_n(P\otimes Q)$ sits in a short exact sequence between the cokernel of $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}\iota\otimes1$ and the kernel of $\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\iota\otimes1$ (the splicing lemma of [[homological-algebra]]). Since $0\to B_p\to Z_p\to H_p(P)\to0$ is a free resolution, the cokernel of $\iota\otimes1\colon B_p\otimes H_q(Q)\to Z_p\otimes H_q(Q)$ is $H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)$ by right exactness, and its kernel is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_p(P),H_q(Q))$ by definition. For the splitting (exercise), first suppose $Q$ is free too. Retractions $P_p\to Z_p$ and $Q_q\to Z_q(Q)$ exist because the boundaries are free, and composing them with the projections to homology gives chain maps $P\to H(P)$ and $Q\to H(Q)$ into complexes with zero differential; their tensor product induces $H_n(P\otimes Q)\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)$, which is a left inverse of the first map. For general $Q$, choose for each $q$ a free resolution $0\to R_q\to E_q\to H_q(Q)\to0$, lift $E_q\to H_q(Q)$ to $E_q\to Z_q(Q)$ and then $R_q\to Q_{q+1}$; this gives a complex of free groups $Q'$ with a quasi-isomorphism $Q'\to Q$, and by naturality of the sequence and the five lemma $H_n(P\otimes Q')\cong H_n(P\otimes Q)$ compatibly with both outer terms. A retraction of $P_p\to Z_p$ alone does not suffice when $Q$ is not free, because $H_p(P)\otimes H_q(Q)\to H_q(H_p(P)\otimes Q)$ need not be injective.

blocks.title: A tensor square with a Tor class
blocks.body: Let $C$ be the complex $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $2,1,0$, the cellular chain complex of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ (used again in the universal coefficient exercises on [[ext]]), with $H_0 = \mathbb{Z}$, $H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, $H_2 = 0$. Compute $H_n(C\otimes C)$.
blocks.solution:
By the Künneth formula, the tensor part in degree $n$ is $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p\otimes H_q$ and the Tor part is $\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\mathrm{Tor}(H_p,H_q)$; only $\mathrm{Tor}(H_1,H_1) = \mathrm{Tor}(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ is non-zero among the Tor groups, since $H_0$ is free and $H_2 = 0$.

$H_0 = \mathbb{Z}\otimes\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}$. $H_1 = H_0\otimes H_1\oplus H_1\otimes H_0 = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$. $H_2 = H_1\otimes H_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$, with no Tor contribution. $H_3$: the tensor part $H_1\otimes H_2\oplus H_2\otimes H_1$ is $0$, and the Tor part is $\mathrm{Tor}(H_1,H_1) = \mathbb{Z}/2$. $H_4 = 0$.

So $H_\bullet(C\otimes C) = \mathbb{Z},(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2,\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0$. The class in degree $3$ is invisible to $H_\bullet(C)\otimes H_\bullet(C)$: with $e_i$ the generator of $C_i$, the element $e_2\otimes e_1+e_1\otimes e_2$ has boundary $2e_1\otimes e_1-2e_1\otimes e_1 = 0$ by the sign rule, while $d(e_2\otimes e_2) = 2(e_1\otimes e_2+e_2\otimes e_1)$, so it is a cycle of order $2$. The checks confirm the whole computation with a Smith normal form. The topological Künneth theorem for a product of spaces needs, in addition, that the chains on $X\times Y$ are chain equivalent to the tensor product of the chains; that belongs to the [[cohomology]] page.

blocks.body:
1. Use the Künneth formula to compute $H_\bullet(C\otimes D)$ for $C = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{4}\mathbb{Z})$ and $D = (\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{6}\mathbb{Z})$, both in degrees $1,0$, and compare with the total-complex example in the balancing section of [[derived-functors]].
2. Prove that the Künneth sequence splits when $P$ is a complex of free abelian groups.

blocks.title: Reading the papers
blocks.body:
Three of the papers in this series use Tor directly.

1. Holanda and Miranda-Neto, Cohen-Macaulay Burch rings. Tor of finitely generated modules over a Noetherian local ring, and its vanishing as a hypothesis (Tor: definition and first computations; computing Tor in practice). The freeness criterion through $\mathrm{Tor}_1(M,k)$ and Betti numbers is in the section on minimal resolutions of [[ext]], and their Ext-Tor dualities are in the tools for Ext there.
2. Tang, profinite and solid cohomology. Tor requires resolutions and flatness, and the remark that projective modules need not be flat in non-classical settings, so that Tor must be computed by resolving both variables (pitfalls below; the balancing theorem itself is on [[derived-functors]]).
3. Shekhar and Gupta, Tor-vanishing of local rings. Tor of finitely generated modules over a Noetherian local ring and its symmetry (Tor: definition and first computations), the fact that $\mathrm{Tor}_i^R(M,N) = 0$ for $i>\mathrm{pd}_RM$ and the Tor-vanishing property (computing Tor in practice, item 4), the Betti numbers $\beta_n^R(M) = \dim_k\mathrm{Tor}_n^R(k,M)$ of a minimal free resolution and the projective dimension (the section on minimal resolutions of [[ext]]; use the symmetry of Tor to swap the arguments), and the Koszul complex, here only in two variables (the Koszul complex example). Not here: Poincaré series and curvature, the Koszul complex on a minimal generating set of the maximal ideal in general, Golod and generalised Golod rings, DG algebras and Massey operations, complete intersections and Gorenstein rings.

- Projective implies flat for modules, but Tang points out that this can fail in non-classical settings such as solid modules, where Tor must then be computed by resolving both variables.
- Flat is weaker than projective: $\mathbb{Q}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ but not projective. Finitely presented flat modules are projective (Weibel Theorem 3.2.7).
- The symmetry $\mathrm{Tor}_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}_n(B,A)$ is not formal. It needs the balancing theorem, and Arapura remarks that the argument in one standard textbook is incomplete and points to Weibel's Theorem 2.7.2 instead. For non-commutative $R$ the correct statement is $\mathrm{Tor}^R_n(A,B)\cong\mathrm{Tor}^{R^{op}}_n(B,A)$.

Tor is the left derived functor of the tensor product, so this page builds on [[derived-functors]], and on its balancing theorem for the symmetry of Tor and for resolving the second variable. [[localization]] is the basic example of a flat base change, which is what makes Tor computable locally. The Künneth formula is the algebraic half of the Künneth theorem for spaces on the [[cohomology]] page. [[ext]] uses Tor for minimal resolutions, Betti numbers and Ext-Tor dualities, and the universal coefficient theorem there is the special case of the Künneth formula with a module in place of the second complex.

checks.claim: Tor_1(Z/m,Z/n) (kernel of m on Z/n) and Ext^1(Z/m,Z/n) (cokernel of m on Z/n) both have order gcd(m,n); Tor(Z/4,Z/6)=Z/2
checks.python:
from math import gcd
for m in range(1,31):
    for n in range(1,31):
        ker=[x for x in range(n) if (m*x)%n==0]
        img=set((m*x)%n for x in range(n))
        assert len(ker)==gcd(m,n)
        assert n//len(img)==gcd(m,n)
        # kernel is cyclic: generated by n/d
        d=gcd(m,n); assert sorted(ker)==sorted(set((k*(n//d))%n for k in range(d)))
assert len([x for x in range(6) if (4*x)%6==0])==2

checks.claim: Koszul resolution of k over k[x,y]: composite is zero, exact (Hilbert series check), and Tor_i(k,k) has dimensions 1,2,1
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
x,y,t=sp.symbols('x y t')
d1=sp.Matrix([[x,y]]); d2=sp.Matrix([[-y],[x]])
assert sp.expand(d1*d2)==sp.zeros(1,1)
# graded Euler characteristic: H(k)= H(R) - 2t H(R) + t^2 H(R) with H(R)=1/(1-t)^2
HR=1/(1-t)**2
assert sp.simplify(HR*(1-2*t+t**2)-1)==0
# tensor with k: set x=y=0, all differentials vanish
assert d1.subs({x:0,y:0})==sp.zeros(1,2) and d2.subs({x:0,y:0})==sp.zeros(2,1)
assert [sp.binomial(2,i) for i in range(3)]==[1,2,1]
# exactness at R^2 in low degrees by linear algebra: kernel of (f,g)->xf+yg in degree<=4 equals image of h->(-yh,xh)
from itertools import product
def monos(deg): return [x**i*y**(deg-i) for i in range(deg+1)]
for D in range(0,5):
    # (f,g) of degree D maps to degree D+1; h of degree D-1
    basis=[(m,0) for m in monos(D)]+[(0,m) for m in monos(D)]
    tgt=monos(D+1)
    M=sp.Matrix([[sp.Poly(x*f+y*g,x,y).coeff_monomial(mm) for (f,g) in basis] for mm in tgt]) if D>=0 else None
    kerdim=len(basis)-M.rank()
    imdim=len(monos(D-1)) if D>=1 else 0
    assert kerdim==imdim

checks.claim: Tor over k[x,y] of k with R/(x): complex k[y] -> k[y]^2 -> k[y] with matrices (-y,0)^T and (0,y) has homology k, k, 0
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
y=sp.symbols('y')
a=sp.Matrix([[-y],[0]]); b=sp.Matrix([[0,y]])
assert b*a==sp.zeros(1,1)
# degree-wise over k in degrees <= 6 of the source: H0 = k[y]/(y) dim 1; H1 = {(f,0)}/{(-yh,0)} dim 1; H2 = ker a = 0
def dimH(deg):
    # H0 in degree deg: k[y]_deg modulo y*k[y]_{deg-1}
    h0 = 1 - (1 if deg>=1 else 0)
    # H1: kernel of (f,g)->y g in degree deg is {(f,0)} dim 1; image of h (deg-1) -> (-y h,0) has dim 1 if deg>=1
    h1 = 1 - (1 if deg>=1 else 0)
    return h0,h1
tot0=sum(dimH(d)[0] for d in range(7)); tot1=sum(dimH(d)[1] for d in range(7))
assert tot0==1 and tot1==1

from math import gcd
I,J=4,6
lcm=I*J//gcd(I,J)
assert (I*J)//lcm==2 and gcd(I,J)==2
for a in range(1,20):
    for b in range(1,20):
        l=a*b//gcd(a,b); assert (a*b)//l==gcd(a,b)

checks.claim: Intersection multiplicity: dim_k k[x,y]/(y, y-x^2) = 2, and y-x^2 is a non-zero-divisor on k[x,y]/(y)=k[x]
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
x,y=sp.symbols('x y')
G=sp.groebner([y, y-x**2], x, y, order='lex')
# standard monomials: those not divisible by leading terms
lts=[sp.Poly(g,x,y).monoms()[0] for g in G.exprs]
std=[(i,j) for i in range(5) for j in range(5) if not any(i>=a and j>=b for (a,b) in lts)]
assert len(std)==2
# on k[x], y-x^2 acts as -x^2 which is injective (degree raises)
f=sp.Poly(-x**2,x)
for d in range(5):
    assert (f*sp.Poly(x**d,x)).degree()==d+2

checks.claim: Tor^{k[x,y]}_i(k, k[x,y]/(x)): the complex k[y] -> k[y]^2 -> k[y] with maps h->(-yh,0) and (f,g)->yg has homology dimensions 1,1,0, computed degree by degree
checks.python:
import sympy as sp
y=sp.symbols('y')
def vec(p,deg):
    P=sp.Poly(p,y); return [P.coeff_monomial(y**i) for i in range(deg)]
# truncate: C2 = polys of degree < D, C1 = pairs of degree <= D, C0 = degree <= D+1 (maps raise degree by one, so the truncation is a subcomplex with the same homology)
D=6
def basis(n): return [y**i for i in range(n)]
# C2 = k[y]_{<D}, C1 = (k[y]_{<D+1})^2, C0 = k[y]_{<D+2}
M2=sp.zeros(2*(D+1),D)
for j,h in enumerate(basis(D)):
    v=vec(-y*h,D+1);
    for i in range(D+1): M2[i,j]=v[i]
M1=sp.zeros(D+2,2*(D+1))
for j in range(D+1):
    v=vec(y*y**j,D+2)
    for i in range(D+2): M1[i,(D+1)+j]=v[i]
assert M1*M2==sp.zeros(D+2,D)
h2=D-M2.rank()
h1=(2*(D+1)-M1.rank())-M2.rank()
h0=(D+2)-M1.rank()
assert (h2,h1,h0)==(0,1,1)

checks.claim: Kunneth: for C = (Z -2-> Z -0-> Z) in degrees 2,1,0, the total complex C tensor C (with the sign (-1)^p) has homology Z, (Z/2)^2, Z/2, Z/2, 0 in degrees 0..4, matching sum H_p tensor H_q plus sum Tor(H_p,H_q) over p+q=n-1

The splitting remark after the Kunneth proof: for Q = (Z/4 -> Z/2) in degrees 1,0 and A = Z/2, the map H_1(Q) tensor A = Z/2 -> H_1(Q tensor A) = 0 is not injective; and for A = Z + Z/2 the torsion of Hom(A,C^x) is infinite while Ext^1(A,Z) = Z/2
checks.python:
# Q: Q_1 = Z/4 -> Q_0 = Z/2 (reduction), A = Z/2.  H_1(Q) = ker = {0,2} = Z/2, so H_1(Q) (x) A = Z/2.
# Q (x) A: Z/4 (x) Z/2 = Z/2 -> Z/2 (x) Z/2 = Z/2, induced map is the identity, so H_1(Q (x) A) = 0.
H1=[a for a in range(4) if a%2==0]
assert len(H1)==2                      # H_1(Q) = Z/2, and Z/2 (x) Z/2 = Z/2 is nonzero
# Z/m (x) Z/n = Z/gcd; the induced map Z/4(x)Z/2 -> Z/2(x)Z/2 sends class of 1 to class of 1
import math
assert math.gcd(4,2)==2 and math.gcd(2,2)==2
f={a%2:(a%2) for a in range(4)}        # on Z/4 (x) Z/2 = Z/2: a mod 2 -> a mod 2
ker=[k for k in f if f[k]==0]
assert ker==[0]                         # injective, so H_1(Q (x) Z/2) = 0
# hence H_1(Q) (x) Z/2 = Z/2 -> H_1(Q (x) Z/2) = 0 is not injective
# Krulewski's form vs Ext for A = Z + Z/2: Ext^1(A,Z) = Z/2 (2 elements), while Tors Hom(A, C^x) contains
# mu_k x {+-1} for every k, so it is infinite
import cmath
elts=set()
for k in range(1,30):
    z=cmath.exp(2j*cmath.pi/k)
    for s in (1,-1): elts.add((round(z.real,9),round(z.imag,9),s))
assert len(elts)>2
